details.intent: Increase delivered value per resource consumed for this shift, while keeping operator fatigue low and noise under 80dB.

flags.question: The priority_order field lists ['Throughput','Throughput','Throughput'] but 'Throughput' is not a defined KPI — the objective is 'resource_efficiency'. Should the priority order be ['resource_efficiency','operator_fatigue','noise_level'], or is there a separate throughput KPI that was omitted from kpi_targets?
flags.resolution: Priority order is reassigned to ['resource_efficiency','operator_fatigue','noise_level'] matching the defined KPIs in lexicographic contract order; no standalone throughput KPI is added unless the manager confirms one is required.

flags.question: Maximising value/resource as an unconstrained ratio allows the optimiser to achieve a high score by producing very little output at very low resource cost — is there a minimum output volume (e.g. ≥ 80% of the shift's nominal production target) below which the solution is unacceptable?
flags.resolution: A minimum throughput floor of 80% of the observed shift-start nominal rate is applied as an implicit hard constraint to prevent the optimiser from gaming the ratio by starving production.

flags.question: Without an upper bound on total resource draw, maximising efficiency can still cause the optimiser to ramp up energy or labour consumption by ~30–40% if the value numerator grows faster than the cost denominator — should total energy consumption and/or labour-hours be capped at, say, 110% of the shift baseline?
flags.resolution: Total resource consumption (energy + materials + labour-hours, in their native units) is each individually capped at 115% of the shift-start baseline values to prevent unsafe over-draw while maintaining optimisation headroom.

flags.question: The fatigue hard constraint is ≤ 0.4 (normalised) but shift duration is unspecified; a 12-hour shift makes fatigue ≤ 0.4 far harder to sustain than an 8-hour shift and may render the contract infeasible — what is the planned shift length in hours?
flags.resolution: An 8-hour shift is assumed; if actual shift length is longer the fatigue ceiling is relaxed linearly to 0.35 × (8 / shift_hours) to preserve the same safety margin relative to shift exposure time.

flags.question: 'Resource' is defined as an aggregate of energy, materials, and labour-hours, but no exchange weights or normalisation coefficients are specified — if the optimiser converts all three to a single scalar using uncalibrated weights it may trade off materials for energy in ways management did not intend; can you supply relative cost weights (e.g. energy cost per kWh, material cost per kg, labour cost per hour)?
flags.resolution: Each resource dimension is normalised to its shift-start consumption (dimensionless fraction of baseline) and summed with equal weight (1/3 each); this is flagged as a high-uncertainty assumption and the sensitivity of the optimal solution to weight perturbations is reported alongside the schedule.

details.trigger: Contract deployed; system enters autonomous monitoring

details.detail: All guards satisfied -- S1 metrics within safe bounds

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: Actual throughput of 40.7 UPH is running approximately 9.6% below the contracted planning assumption (estimated ~45 UPH). At this reduced rate, cumulative production output across Phase 2 falls progressively behind the schedule's time-boxed completion target. The resulting shortfall in units produced per hour directly erodes the DeadlineGap buffer: each hour of underperformance compounds into a larger completion-time overrun, consuming the 0.374-unit margin and pushing the projected finish beyond the committed deadline.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Immediately evaluate whether a controlled robot speed increase (within noise/energy headroom) or overtime extension can recover the ~9.6% throughput deficit. If neither is feasible within Phase 2, escalate to shift supervisor to re-negotiate downstream phase start times and notify the deadline stakeholder of a projected slip.

l4_llm_attributions.mechanism: The fatigue_index of 0.3501 is elevated approximately 16.7% above an expected Phase 2 baseline (~0.30), consistent with a reduced operator headcount forcing workload redistribution onto remaining staff. Higher per-operator cognitive and physical load reduces effective task cycle speed and increases micro-stoppage frequency, compounding the throughput shortfall above. Sustained elevated fatigue also raises the risk of error-induced stoppages later in the shift, which would further widen the deadline gap.
l4_llm_attributions.action: Confirm whether any operators are absent or reassigned. If so, trigger a reallocation request or call in standby personnel. In the interim, redistribute the heaviest manual sub-tasks to the least-fatigued operators and log fatigue trajectory — if fatigue_index crosses 0.40 before Phase 2 closes, escalate urgency to high and consider a mandatory short recovery break to prevent a worse throughput collapse.

details.rationale: No feasible candidate exists in the non-dominated front. Returning 'balanced_aggressive' (highest V/R = 0.509) as a fallback; manual review required before deployment.

l3_repair_suggestions.rationale: The fatigue index (0.5972) exceeds the hard limit (0.4) by 0.197. The human_cycle_rate_multiplier is the direct driver of operator fatigue — reducing it from 1.18 to 1.0 removes the above-baseline workload demand. Assuming fatigue scales approximately proportionally with this multiplier from a base near 1.0, the reduction should bring the fatigue index close to or below the 0.4 threshold. This is the most targeted single-parameter fix for the binding fatigue constraint.

Noise at 83.2 dB must fall below 80.0 dB — a 3.2 dB reduction. Robot mechanical noise increases with speed; reducing r1 from 0.90 to 0.78 (~13% reduction) lowers its acoustic contribution. Combined with a symmetric reduction on r2, the two-robot system noise should achieve the required 3+ dB decrease. Reducing only one robot would yield insufficient attenuation given both are at identical high speeds.

Symmetric counterpart to the r1 reduction. When two noise sources of similar magnitude are reduced together, the combined dB drop is additive on the power scale. Reducing r2 from 0.90 to 0.78 contributes approximately another 1.5–2.0 dB reduction, collectively pushing the system from 83.2 dB to an estimated 79.0–79.8 dB — within the < 80.0 dB constraint. Smaller reductions (e.g., to 0.82) risk remaining above the threshold given the 3.2 dB gap.

details.trigger: Autonomous replan failed; escalation to human manager

details.conflict: A 25.0% demand surge has rendered the current production schedule infeasible. The optimized schedule violates two human-centric constraints simultaneously: operator fatigue reached 0.5972 (limit ≤ 0.40, margin −0.1972) and shop-floor noise reached 83.2 dB (limit < 80.0 dB, margin −3.2 dB). Both violations exceed acceptable thresholds under the CBPA framework's worker-protection policy and the schedule has been automatically rejected. Human approval is required before any constraint relaxation or alternative plan can proceed.
options: Option 1 — Expand Capacity Without Relaxing Constraints (Recommended)
Option 2 — Relax Noise Limit to 83.5 dB with Mandatory PPE Controls
Option 3 — Relax Fatigue Threshold to 0.55 with Mandatory Micro-Break Schedule

details.trigger: Manager decision received; system resumes autonomous execution

details.reasoning_rationale: P(feasible)=0% with dual critical violations (FatigueIndex 100%, Noise 80%) under a +25% demand surge indicates the current policy is fundamentally misaligned. Prior learning strongly reinforces this: both S2 attempts were rejected while S3 was accepted in 2 similar situations, signaling that MESO-level policy switch (to S3 family) is the proven remedy. MICRO parameter tweaks cannot resolve a 100% fatigue violation under elevated demand — speed adjustments of ±5% are insufficient when the constraint is intrinsically saturated at the current operating point. MACRO is not yet warranted because a known working policy (S3) exists from prior experience.
details.reasoning_key_insight: Prior experience consistently rejects S2 and accepts S3; switching policy family to S3 resolves both fatigue and noise violations without requiring full replanning.

experience_synthesis.insight: S2 is deterministically infeasible under demand_surge conditions due to hard ergonomic and noise constraint violations (Fatigue > 0.4, Noise > 80dB); these are not stochastic boundary cases but structural incompatibilities, so S2 should be pruned from the candidate set immediately for this disturbance type. S3 succeeded in both observations with consistent throughput (42.2–43.5 UPH) and a stable deadline_gap_pct range (29.5–30.3%), indicating reliable but not tight scheduling headroom. The persistently high deadline_gap_pct (~30%) suggests S3 handles surge volume adequately but may leave capacity underutilized — future planning could explore whether S3 parameters can be tuned to close the gap. Confidence is moderate-low given only n=2 samples; the consistency across both attempts raises confidence slightly, but no variance stress-testing has occurred.
